When "vaulting" is used as an adjective, it describes an ambition, desire, or aspiration that is so extreme, so aggressively overreaching, that it goes well beyond what is reasonable or even safely achievable. It doesn't just mean "very ambitious" — it carries a deeper charge. It implies a recklessness, a dangerous excess. The thing being described has stretched itself so far past its limits that it risks toppling over from the sheer force of its own reach.

It almost always appears in a negative or cautionary light. You are not celebrating the ambition — you are flagging it as something alarming, something that has gone too far.

To truly feel what this word means, picture a pole vaulter. They sprint, plant the pole, and hurl themselves into the air — an explosive, dramatic leap over the bar. Now imagine someone vaulting so aggressively, so recklessly, that they sail right over the bar and crash down on the far side. That image — of leaping so powerfully that you overshoot and fall — is the spirit of this word. "Vaulting" ambition doesn't stop at the goal. It flies past it and brings itself down.

This is important: the word doesn't just describe size. It describes a quality of overreach — a reach so extreme that failure or ruin is baked into it.
What It Is Usually Paired With

"Vaulting" almost always modifies abstract nouns — things you cannot touch, but deeply feel:

Vaulting ambition — This is by far the most common and famous use. It describes ambition so fierce and unchecked that it overreaches itself. It's the kind of ambition that makes someone burn every bridge, cross every line, and ultimately destroy themselves in the pursuit of power or success. Shakespeare used this exact phrase in Macbeth to describe Macbeth's drive to become king — a drive so extreme that it led him to murder and ruin.

Vaulting pride — A pride so enormous it makes someone blind to their own failures, unable to accept limits, and contemptuous of others. It is pride on the verge of a fall.

Vaulting ego — An ego so inflated it has lost its connection to reality.

Vaulting desire / vaulting aspirations — Wanting something with such ferocity that the wanting itself becomes the danger.

Notice the pattern: in every case, the word isn't praising the quality. It is quietly warning you that this quality has grown monstrous.

"Vaulting" is not neutral. It carries a tone of unease, of foreboding. When someone calls an ambition "vaulting," they are not cheering for it — they are watching it with concern, the way you'd watch someone lean too far over a railing. There is something almost tragic about it. The word implies that what is being described carries the seeds of its own destruction. It is magnificent and dangerous at the same time.

This is what separates "vaulting" from simpler words like "great" or "strong" or even "ambitious." Those words can be compliments. "Vaulting" is a diagnosis.
How It Feels in a Sentence

Here are examples that show the word doing its real work:

  • His vaulting ambition made him willing to sacrifice his closest friends for a chance at the top.

(The ambition is so out of control, it has consumed his humanity.)

  • She had the talent to succeed, but her vaulting pride refused to let her ask for help — and that was her undoing.

(The pride didn't just make her confident. It made her blind and ultimately caused her failure.)

  • The CEO's vaulting ego led him to make decisions no one around him dared to question — until the company collapsed.

(The ego has grown so extreme it silenced all reason around it.)

  • The young general's vaulting desire for glory pushed him to take risks that no wise soldier would take.

(The desire has passed bold and entered reckless.)

In every example, something has grown so large it has broken free of wisdom, caution, or humanity — and is hurtling toward a fall.

"Vaulting" does not simply mean "large," "strong," or "impressive." A great leader can have immense, powerful ambition — but if it is disciplined and wise, you would not call it vaulting. The word specifically requires that dangerous excess, that sense of overreach. Without the recklessness and the implied downfall, the word doesn't fit.

It is also not the same as "arrogant," though they can overlap. Arrogance is about how someone treats others — looking down on them. Vaulting is about how someone relates to their own limits — refusing to accept them at all.

Outside its figurative life, "vaulting" can occasionally appear in a more physical or visual sense — describing something that leaps dramatically or arches powerfully through space. A phrase like "the vaulting arches of a cathedral ceiling" describes arches that soar upward in a sweeping, dramatic curve. Or you might read of "a vaulting leap" in a poem to describe an animal springing through the air. These uses are far less common, and in everyday reading or writing you are almost certain to encounter "vaulting" in its figurative sense — attached to ambition, pride, ego, or desire.

If you need to carry just one idea with you: vaulting describes an ambition, pride, or desire that has grown so extreme and so reckless that it overreaches itself — leaping so far and so high that it is headed, inevitably, for a fall.
